blokken: Accountants, solicitors, consultants and agencies sell knowledge and time. That makes AI for professional services firms more interesting than for almost any other sector, and more sensitive at the same time. Here's where the gains sit by profession, which kinds of tools exist, and how to protect confidentiality and quality.

Where does the gain from AI for professional services firms sit, and what does it ask of confidentiality?

AI for professional services firms mainly speeds up the reading, analysing and writing that accountants, solicitors, consultants and agencies spend many hours on: AI produces a first draft or a shortlist, the professional judges it and stays accountable for the final result. The choice of tool follows from confidentiality requirements: no client files in free tools, a checked data processing agreement, and firm-wide rules on what's allowed.
Can a DPIA be required for AI for professional services firms?

Yes, for high-risk processing, a Data Protection Impact Assessment for AI for professional services firms is required under UK GDPR, Article 35. With personal data, firms should check whether a DPIA is needed, and the data processing agreement, storage location and training-on-data terms should be checked too.
What does the choice of tool depend on for AI for professional services firms?

On the tasks, the existing software and the data-processing requirements, which tool fits for AI for professional services firms depends, not on the most impressive demo. Specialised tools offer more domain depth, but need a check on the sourcing of references and the pricing model.

Why AI pays off for professional services firms

Most of what a professional services firm does is reading, analysing and writing. Searching through files, summarising documents, drafting reports, writing correspondence. That’s exactly what generative AI is good at. AI for professional services firms is therefore less about robots and more about speeding up the knowledge-intensive work that currently costs hours.
There are three reasons this sector benefits in particular:
Volume. Many tasks come up dozens of times a week in a similar form, such as a memo, a review or a report.
An existing check step. In most firms, a senior colleague already reviews work before it goes out. That review is the most important safeguard you need.
Scarcity. Good professionals are hard to find. Time freed up from routine work can go towards advice, client contact or mentoring juniors.

There’s a caveat too. Anyone billing by the hour needs to think through what time savings mean for the business model. And professional reputation is on the line: one mistake in advice to a client weighs heavier than ten hours saved.
The professional rules differ, but the pattern is the same: AI delivers a first draft or a shortlist, the professional judges it.

In accountancy, the opportunities sit in processing and checking large volumes of data and documents: reading and coding records, flagging anomalies and unusual transactions, reviewing contracts and drafting commentary on figures. ICAEW’s guidance applies the IESBA Code’s five fundamental principles to the use of technology, including generative AI, and names threats such as over-reliance on tools and limited understanding of how they work (ICAEW, Generative AI guide). The common thread: validation and professional judgement remain the basis.
For smaller accountancy practices, client communication is added to that: answering business owners’ questions and translating annual figures into plain language.

Solicitors and lawyers use AI to search and summarise case files and case law, compare contract versions, flag unusual clauses, and draft documents. This is exactly where the check step matters most: a language model can confidently cite cases that don’t exist.

The Solicitors Regulation Authority issued a warning notice on the misuse of AI in August 2026, following dozens of reports of potential misuse in the preceding twelve months. It flagged two areas in particular: fabricated content, such as invented cases and citations, and client confidentiality, including the risk that free or inadequately secured AI tools compromise legal professional privilege (HSF Kramer summary of the notice). The solicitor stays accountable for the final advice at all times.

Consultants and agencies spend a lot of time on research, processing interviews, structuring analysis and writing reports. AI helps structure interview notes, search past projects, draft a first report structure, and rewrite a proposal for a new client’s context.

The risk here is complacency: reports that sound good but say little. The value of a consultant sits in judgement and choice, and that can’t be outsourced. How one professional services firm introduced an internal AI assistant built around a handful of fixed scenarios is covered in the case study on an AI assistant for knowledge workers.

An accountancy practice with 45 staff produces around 400 compiled financial statements a year. Assistants currently spend an average of three hours per file reading records and drafting a first commentary.

The consultant helps the practice choose a business AI assistant with a data processing agreement and clear terms on storage and training on data, tested on 20 anonymised files. The partners agree that a senior colleague keeps reviewing every commentary, exactly as happens now.

After one season, preparation takes an average of two hours per file, around 400 fewer hours a year. Because the practice charges a fixed fee for this work, that time goes straight to margin; under an hourly rate the sums would look different. Deliberately not done: using AI on statutory audit work. The practice wants its own approach, based on professional-body guidance, in place first.
Illustrative example, built from situations that come up often. The organisation and figures are for illustration.
For professional services firms there are broadly three kinds of tools, each with a different trade-off:
General AI assistantBroadly useful for text and summarising. Choose a business licence with clear terms on your data.
AI in existing softwareFeatures inside your practice management, case or accounting software. Works within the environment where your data already sits.
Specialised toolsBuilt for legal, tax or audit work. More domain depth, but check the sourcing of its references and the pricing model.
The closer a tool sits to your profession and your existing data, the greater the value, but also the more important the selection.

Which tool fits depends on your tasks, your existing software and your data-processing requirements, not the most impressive demo. An overview of the kinds of tools and how to choose between them is on AI tools for business. Firms running Microsoft 365 will find more depth in Microsoft Copilot for business.

When choosing, pay particular attention to: where your data is stored and processed, whether your input is used to train the model, how the tool handles sourcing, and what it costs to switch away again.
For a professional services firm, confidentiality isn’t an afterthought, it’s the starting point. A few ground rules:

No client files in free tools. The less you pay, the more likely your data is being used in some other way. The Solicitors Regulation Authority’s warning notice makes this point explicitly for free or inadequately secured tools.

Read the contract, not the brochure. Check the data processing agreement, the storage location and the terms on training on your data. For personal data, check whether a Data Protection Impact Assessment is required; under UK GDPR, Article 35, it’s mandatory for high-risk processing.
Set firm-wide rules. Without a policy, every member of staff develops their own approach. How to set that up without creating bureaucracy is covered under AI policy for organisations.
Match the check to the risk. An internal note needs a lighter review than advice, an opinion or a document going to court or a regulator.
Keep sources checkable. Prefer tools that show where an answer comes from, and always verify references against the original source.
Protecting quality also means measuring it. Pick a few tasks, record upfront how long they take and how many corrections they need, and compare that with AI after a few weeks.

Working mostly with numbers and reporting? AI and BI is also worth a look. Running a small firm? See AI for small business too. The broader picture is on AI for business. Want to talk through the first step for your practice? Book a call.

Do I need to tell clients I'm using AI?+

Transparency is sensible and fits a relationship of trust. The Solicitors Regulation Authority's 2026 warning notice on AI use expects firms to be clear about how they use AI and to safeguard client confidentiality when they do. Outside law, it also helps to set out how you use AI in your engagement letter or terms.
What if AI gets something wrong in my advice?+

Then it's your mistake. The professional stays accountable for the final result, even if a tool drafted it. Set up a check step that matches the risk: a quick look for an internal note, a substantive review for anything that goes to a client.
Does AI change our business model?+

It can. If work you bill by the hour goes faster, time saved under an hourly rate earns you less, unless you put the freed-up time towards other billable work or move more towards fixed fees. Build that question into your business case, not just after the fact.
Can a small firm get started with AI too?+

Yes. A small firm can start with a business licence on an AI assistant and a handful of fixed tasks, such as summarising and draft correspondence. Decide upfront what data must never go in, and who checks the result.
